finding.claim: Amount is not validated as a finite number. JSON NaN is accepted by Python's json parser. With amount=NaN, both `amount <= 0` and `BAL < amount` evaluate False, so the guards pass. The balance becomes NaN, and every later `BAL < x` check is False, so the account has unlimited withdrawals and transfers. The same holds in /transfer. Non-numeric types (a string or a list) cause an unhandled TypeError and a 500.

finding.claim: The balance check and the debit are not atomic (TOCTOU race). Concurrent requests can each pass the check before any debit runs, so a user can withdraw or transfer more than their balance. The global in-memory dict has no lock, and the app may run multi-threaded or with multiple worker processes. With multiple processes each worker has its own BAL, so state is inconsistent.
finding.source: Concurrent POST /withdraw or /transfer requests from one authenticated user
finding.sink: BAL[g.user] -= amount, executed after the separate check

trace.note: use: the debit happens later with no lock or transaction (transfer)
the same check-then-act pattern in withdraw

finding.guards_checked: No threading.Lock, DB transaction or atomic operation is present. There is no idempotency key and no rate limit. The exploit is practical under a threaded Flask server or gunicorn threads.

verdict.reason: bank.py:11-13 (transfer) and bank.py:21-23 (withdraw) check BAL[g.user] and then debit it in separate statements with no lock, transaction or atomic operation. Any authenticated user can send concurrent requests, so a threaded server can interleave the check and the debit. The race window is only a few bytecodes under the GIL, so it is narrow but real. With multiple workers, each process would also hold its own BAL, which is a separate consistency problem.

finding.claim: /transfer debits the sender before validating the recipient. If `to` is not a key in BAL, BAL[to] raises KeyError and returns a 500, but the sender's debit on line 13 has already been applied and is not rolled back. Funds are destroyed. An attacker can also grief another user, or use a nonexistent account to cause loss in a partially failing flow. There is also no check that `to` is a string, and none that to != g.user.

finding.claim: No authentication is implemented in this code. g.user is read in both handlers but is never assigned anywhere in the repo: there is no before_request hook, login route or token verification.
